Consider, for example, Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī’s explanation of the “purpose of kalām”:

“Its purpose is to preserve the creed of the Sunnis and protect it from the confusion introduced by the people of innovation. (...) Then Satan planted in the minds of the innovators ideas that contradicted the Sunna. They became absorbed in them and came close to disturbing the true belief of its followers. So God raised up a group of theologians and moved them to defend the Sunna through ordered argument, exposing the deceptions of the new innovators who opposed the inherited teaching of the Sunnis. From this arose kalām and its practitioners, and so on.”
If we take al-Ghazālī’s words at face value, then the history of kalām begins only when Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī founded his school in opposition to the Muʿtazila.
Everything the Muʿtazila had written and debated in the field before that point would then have to be erased from the history of kalām.
Ibn Khaldūn follows the same path in his definition. He begins:
“Kalām is a field of knowledge that argues for the beliefs of faith through rational proofs and refutes innovators who depart in their beliefs from the doctrines of the early Muslims and the Sunnis.”

As he explains this definition, it becomes clear that by “innovators who depart in their beliefs from the doctrines of the early Muslims and the Sunnis,” he means the Shiʿa, Murjiʾa, anthropomorphists, Muʿtazila, and Imamis.

He then says that the innovations of these groups and schools created the need “to defend these beliefs with rational proofs against the attacks of these innovations,” and that “Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, the imam of the theologians, undertook this task,” and so on.

Ibn Khaldūn then reviews the questions al-Ashʿarī addressed in his response to these “innovators and deviants,” and concludes that after the question of the imamate had been added, the whole collection of these questions came to be called kalām.
There can therefore be little doubt that among the Ashʿarites, the term kalām had a particular meaning and a particular content that applied only to Ashʿarite theology.
The same was true of the term mutakallimūn, “theologians,” which was likewise restricted to Ashʿarite theologians.
This removes from the history of kalām all the rational thought based on philosophical reflection that appeared before Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī.

It also excludes all the creative rationalist theologians of that earlier period who helped prepare the way for Arab-Islamic philosophy. At an early stage in its intellectual awakening, they trained Arab-Islamic thought to work with abstraction, concepts, and categories.
We have no objection to the Ashʿarites choosing whatever names and terms they wish for their own school and their own thought.
But we do object when they cut away part of the history of kalām so completely that the field appears to begin and end with them.
We should therefore set aside the claims of both the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites that kalām belongs exclusively within the boundaries of their own particular school.
Instead, we must look at history and historical reality as they actually developed, in all their dimensions.

If we do this, and follow the long history of kalām from Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ (d. 131 AH/748 CE), the founder of the Muʿtazilite school, to Ibn Taymiyya (661–728 AH/thirteenth–fourteenth centuries CE), one of the best-known later traditionalist theologians, two basic conclusions emerge.

First, kalām includes the whole range of questions framed in religious and doctrinal terms that arose from different forms of social and political conflict in Arab-Islamic society from the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs onward.

Over time, these questions were transformed into complex ideas about the world beyond nature. Their original social dimensions became almost hidden behind a fog of abstractions. Alongside these appeared views with a philosophical direction concerning the natural world, though still approached from a theological point of view.
Many different schools and tendencies of kalām appeared during this long history. Yet the basic questions they discussed and disputed remained largely the same.

And if we look beyond the outward form of the ideas, the deepest reasons for disagreement over each of these questions—whether individually or as a whole—were always rooted in social reality. At their deepest level, they arose from the position occupied by the supporters of these ideas within the wider social structure of their society.
Second, kalām passed through two main stages during this history of roughly six centuries: a Muʿtazilite stage and an Ashʿarite stage.
This division does not mean that we have forgotten the many theological ideas and debates that belonged to neither school.

The Imami Shiʿa, for example, developed their own theological positions, especially on the question of the imamate. The Kharijites, Murjiʾa, Jahmite determinists, those who likened God to created beings, those who described God in bodily terms, the incarnationists, and later traditionalists such as Ibn Taymiyya all developed views of their own.
Our division into two stages is based instead on the main direction taken by kalām across its history as a whole.

If we study kalām according to its broad intellectual and ideological direction, we are led to this conclusion: its history was dominated by two major tendencies, forming two stages that were opposed to one another just as Muʿtazilite thought was opposed to Ashʿarite thought.
A — The Muʿtazilite Stage of Kalām
We can say that the Ashʿarite stage was, in a sense, a reaction against the Muʿtazilite stage.
From its beginnings and throughout its development, the Muʿtazilite movement had two striking features.
The first was its opposition to traditionalist thought and ideology.
The second was the method it used in carrying out that opposition.

That method was itself the revolutionary side of the movement. It was a rationalist method whose most distinctive aim was to examine every question of Islamic metaphysics through reason and to give the human mind the leading role in the search for knowledge.

But this rationalist approach itself grew out of another question that, under the historical conditions of the time, was perhaps even more closely connected with social reality: the freedom of the human mind to think without being bound by a predetermined fate, and, through this, the freedom of the human will to act without being constrained by a will that had already decided everything in advance.
Looking at the Muʿtazilite movement through these closely connected questions allows us to see its historically revolutionary character.
It is true that the Muʿtazila usually dealt with theological questions through abstract rational reflection.
This tendency became stronger as they came into closer contact with Greek philosophy and as the questions before them became more numerous, varied, and complex.
It is also true that Muʿtazilite thought remained deeply marked by theology, even when it dealt with the natural world—for example, in discussions of the indivisible particle, or atomism.
But first, this reflected the historical conditions themselves: religious knowledge dominated intellectual life, and Islam exerted a powerful influence throughout society.
Second, under those conditions, no new intellectual movement could have expressed its revolutionary character in any other form or by any other method.

And third, none of this could hide another essential feature of Muʿtazilite thought: its opposition to absolute faith in the unseen, to the idea that faith should come before reason, and to the belief that absolute predestination governs the movement of individuals and society and determines all human choices.
We should also note an important fact about the Muʿtazila’s social position.
The Muʿtazila did not form an independent social class or group simply by being Muʿtazilites, either under the Umayyads or under the Abbasids.

They belonged instead to a much larger learned group that emerged as Arab-Islamic society developed socially and culturally: the scholars of jurisprudence, Hadith, Qurʾanic commentary, and related fields such as Arabic language studies and logic.

Like Shiʿi, Kharijite, Murjiʾite, and Sunni theologians, every Muʿtazilite scholar of kalām was also counted among the jurists, Hadith scholars, Qurʾanic commentators, grammarians, or often several of these at once.

This large learned group was not separate from the political movements alongside which it existed. In many cases, it formed their religious component. Yet it still had a distinct position within them and exercised a special influence on public opinion.
That position gave it the ability to respond to, and interact with, social and political movements of many different kinds within the wider public.
This is one reason ideological struggle could become just as intense as direct political struggle.

It also helps us understand why the positions taken by the Muʿtazila in the ideological battles of their age were historically necessary and played a real part in the development of society at that stage.
This historical role represents the positive and revolutionary phase of Muʿtazilite kalām.
Its importance did not lie simply in the ideas themselves, but in the historical effect they produced.

That effect was possible, first, because society at the time was receptive to ideas that challenged the ideology of the existing political order, and second, because Muʿtazilite kalām had a particular power of attraction.
Its appeal came from the fact that it confronted the basic principles and questions on which the ideology of the caliphate itself rested.
Its effect in shaking those foundations was stronger than the wars of the Kharijites, despite the violence of those wars—or perhaps, we might say, partly because of that violence.
At this point we face an important question that deserves serious study: the relationship between the Muʿtazila and the power of the caliphate under the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn.
The ruler who occupied the throne at the time embraced Muʿtazilite doctrine so fully that it became the official doctrine of the caliphate for the reigns of three Abbasid caliphs.
This seems to cast doubt on what we have said about Muʿtazilite kalām carrying the banner of intellectual and ideological opposition to state power.

The doubt may seem even stronger because, for more than sixteen years, it was the opponents of the Muʿtazila who carried the banner of opposition, while the Muʿtazila encouraged the state to persecute their opponents, even physically.
Does this mean that the ideology of the state had changed?
Or had the ideology of the Muʿtazila changed?
Our scientific method warns us against making judgments in absolute terms.
An absolute judgment is, by its nature, static and metaphysical. It contradicts both dialectical method and the dynamic movement of life itself.
So we cannot say that every opposition to political authority is necessarily progressive or revolutionary in every respect.
Nor can we say that every existing state power is necessarily reactionary in every respect.

But the particular historical relationship that developed between the Muʿtazila and the Abbasid state under al-Maʾmūn—and continued under al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq—has until now usually been studied from an idealist and subjective point of view.
Researchers have not seriously tried to uncover the economic and social factors lying behind it in the early Abbasid period.

Modern studies often say, for example, that al-Maʾmūn was highly educated, deeply interested in scientific and literary study, philosophically minded, and intellectually open. Because the Muʿtazila were the school most committed to intellectual freedom and reason, their doctrine naturally appealed to him. He therefore brought Muʿtazilites close to him, and they gained influence at court.

If this explains the matter during al-Maʾmūn’s reign, how do we explain the fact that this policy continued for about sixteen years after his death, through the caliphates of al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq, even though neither of them had al-Maʾmūn’s intellectual gifts, learning, or freedom of thought?

This question deserves a full study using the method of historical materialism. Here, however, we can do no more than lay some groundwork for such a study. We will draw on a number of economic and social indicators from the age of al-Maʾmūn, as well as on the general laws that govern the dialectical movement of society.

We cannot simply dismiss the role of al-Maʾmūn himself. He was an educated and intellectually open-minded ruler, and under him the state adopted the Muʿtazilite position on the famous theological question of whether the Qurʾān was created.

What we should reject is the idea that al-Maʾmūn’s personal role was either the main cause or the only cause, rather than one contributing factor, behind this bold move. He officially declared that the caliphal state accepted the Muʿtazilite position on the created Qurʾān despite the opposition of conservative public opinion, especially Sunni jurists, hadith scholars, and Qurʾān commentators. He also made the Muʿtazilite school as a whole the doctrine of the state and punished those who opposed it, sometimes even physically.

The main explanation for this development must be sought in the wider historical conditions in which al-Maʾmūn secured his position on the Abbasid throne at the end of the second and beginning of the third Islamic centuries—that is, in the ninth century CE.

The first thing that stands out is the way he came to power. Al-Maʾmūn reached the caliphate after a bloody struggle between two sets of forces. On one side were the leaders and princes of the feudal forces who supported his brother al-Amīn. On the other were forces rooted in the urban economy and in the commercial, moneylending, and craft-based life of the cities, together with the educated circles that carried freer ideas. These urban forces supported al-Maʾmūn in his struggle for the throne and absolute power.

Trade had flourished during the first period of Abbasid rule. Once Iraq became the center of the caliphate, it also became a meeting point for major international trade routes. Commerce expanded, and many city-dwellers entered trade because of the large profits it offered and the rising social position of merchants.
The Abbasids generally encouraged overseas trade, and this became one of the most important forms of economic activity during the early Abbasid period.

This naturally strengthened certain social groups in the cities, especially in the capital. In feudal societies, these groups grow and begin to play a greater political role whenever conditions favor commercial expansion. Their rise comes partly at the expense of major landowners and the wealthy rural classes. This happens especially when transport is regular, communications are reliable, and foreign markets are active.
Those conditions existed at the time.

The growing urban groups in the Iraqi cities were diverse both socially and ethnically. They were not limited to wealthy merchants and owners of commercial capital. They also included people involved in money capital, lending, and banking; owners of craft workshops and their skilled workers; small traders; shopkeepers; and people engaged in simple forms of buying and selling.
Every one of these groups contained a mixture of Arabs and members of the many other peoples who lived within the Abbasid Empire.

This was especially clear among the ʿāmma—the broad mass of workers and poor people. They included Arabs, Persians, Turks, Zanj, Daylamites, Byzantines, Nabataeans, Armenians, Georgians, Slavs, Kurds, and Berbers. What united them was the dominant common language: Arabic.
This was generally true across the cities of Iraq. Ethnic distinctions seem to have become almost dissolved within this human mixture.
From this we can conclude that a person’s class position in third-century Islamic society could, to some extent, shape their political position as well.

We can see this in the support that many urban social groups gave to al-Maʾmūn’s bid for the Abbasid throne. They did so partly because princes and major landholders had rallied around his brother al-Amīn.

Those princes and leaders hoped to benefit from al-Amīn’s weak personality, his attraction to a life of entertainment, and his lack of interest in the wider affairs of the state. They hoped this would allow them to expand their own power and perhaps even achieve a degree of independence in one region or another of the empire.
Al-Maʾmūn therefore came to supreme power with the backing of social groups whose class interests conflicted with those of the groups tied to rural feudal estates.

Under his rule, the conflict between these forces had to take on a new form. This included a new attitude toward the people who had supported al-Amīn and toward their representatives in intellectual life: the conservative jurists, hadith scholars, and Qurʾān commentators.

This, as we see it, helps explain why the banner of free thought rose so high under al-Maʾmūn in the form of Muʿtazilite kalām. Because the same underlying forces remained strong, that banner continued to fly under his brother al-Muʿtaṣim and then under al-Wāthiq, the son of al-Muʿtaṣim.
